topics.topic: Crash-durable ordering of file publication and database commits
questions: Does “flushed” require durability across host or power failure, including syncing the containing directory after rename, or only completeness across a kernel-process crash?
What exact ordering and durability protocol relates temporary-file flush, rename, directory flush and SQLite commit so a committed record can never name a missing file after a crash?
What does “flushed” guarantee, and what publication, directory-sync and SQLite-commit order prevents a committed record from naming a file that disappears after a crash or power loss?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about publication, flushing, SQLite commit ordering and crash durability judged in P24.

precedent.topic: Filesystem publication, SQLite commit ordering, flushing, and crash durability
quotes:
Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked
   against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is
   never overwritten — a spooled file no record names, left by a change that
   failed, is replaced at its position.
precedent.why: The topic concerns unchanged A18 publication and durability language, which the reopening change did not affect.

topics.topic: Event defining serialization order for concurrent requests
questions: What observable event defines arrival order when requests are received concurrently or become readable at the same time?
At what event is a request considered to have arrived, and how are requests that are concurrently received or become complete together ordered?
Which observable event establishes arrival order when multiple MCP requests arrive concurrently?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the event defining concurrent request arrival order judged in P23.

precedent.topic: Event defining serialized arrival order for concurrent requests
quotes:
Surface requests are handled one at a time in the order they arrive: one request, including the run
   advancement it causes (A13), ends before the next begins, so an approval, a
   cancellation and a resume of one run never race.
precedent.why: The serialization sentence is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect concurrent-request ordering.

topics.topic: Exclusive data-directory locking and stale-lock behavior
questions: What kind of lock establishes exclusivity, and must it be released automatically after a crash rather than leaving a stale marker that blocks future starts?
What object and locking primitive define the lock, how are aliased paths or bind mounts of the same directory recognized, and what happens to a stale lock artifact after a crash?
What object and locking primitive define this lock, when is it acquired and released, and does a stale lock file after a crash prevent startup?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the lock object, primitive, lifetime and stale-lock behavior judged in P30.

precedent.topic: Exclusive-lock object, primitive, lifetime, and failure handling
quotes:
At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data
   directory; a second process on the same directory refuses to start.
precedent.why: The lock requirement is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect its object, primitive or lifetime.

topics.topic: Ownership and permission requirements for private storage
questions: What exact ownership, file types, and permission bits make the data directory and each contained file or directory private?
What exact ownership and access test defines “private” for the directory, nested directories, database and sidecar files, stored values, fixtures, spool files and lock file, including ACLs?
What exact ownership, object-type and permission-bit conditions make the data directory, its subdirectories, database files, lock file, SQLite auxiliary files and stored payloads “private”?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about ownership, object types, permissions, ACLs and hard links for private store data judged in P15.

precedent.topic: Filesystem ownership, type, permissions, ACL, and hard-link requirements for private store data
quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.
precedent.why: The topic concerns A18's unchanged data-directory privacy rule, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change to A17 and A20 did not make that existing question matter.

topics.topic: Required filesystem semantics and behavior on unsupported filesystems
questions: What happens on a Linux filesystem that does not provide the locking, atomic-rename, or durability semantics these guarantees require?
Which filesystem guarantees are required for locking, atomic rename, durable flushes and SQLite transactions, and does startup refuse a filesystem on which A18's crash guarantees cannot be made?

Is conforming behavior required on every Linux host with the named open-flag semantics even when its filesystem lacks the locking, rename, flush or SQLite guarantees A18 needs, or are those also host-support conditions?
Does supported Linux also require a filesystem that provides reliable SQLite locking, atomic same-filesystem rename and durable fsync semantics, and what happens on Linux filesystems that do not?

quotes:
The kernel is one process. At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data
   directory; a second process on the same directory refuses to start.

Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked
   against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is
   never overwritten — a spooled file no record names, left by a change that
   failed, is replaced at its position.

A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another system, or
   a Linux on which an open flag these rules name (`O_NOFOLLOW`, `O_PATH`,
   `O_DIRECTORY`) does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: the
   kernel neither tests for it nor defines what it does there; the sandbox's facilities stay A03's,
   which the start probes.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats every Linux filesystem as supported and proceeds despite inadequate locking, rename, fsync or SQLite semantics; another detects or documents such filesystems as unsupported and refuses startup. The installer and owner notice whether startup succeeds and whether committed records survive crashes without missing files.
judgement.why: The new host rule excludes deficient open-flag semantics but does not say whether deficient filesystem locking, rename, durability or SQLite semantics are likewise unsupported or must be detected.

topics.topic: Assignment and meaning of record positions within a transaction
questions: When one store call creates several records, what determines their distinct positions in the store's one order?

What exactly is a record's store position, and how are positions assigned among several records written by one transaction so activation identity, corpus order, recovery order and pagination are identical in every implementation?

judgement.why: This is the same question about global store-position allocation and within-transaction record ordering decided in P12.

precedent.topic: Store-order assignment for multiple records in one transaction and for updated records
quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Every record written gets one store position from next_store_position, a single strictly increasing counter shared by all record types, called inside the transaction that writes the record; store order is the order of these positions, every collection the module returns is in store order unless the function says otherwise, and Activation and FlowActivation records are identified by their store_position.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] The records one change writes take their store positions with every StoredValue first, in the order the variant names them, then the other records in the order the field-assignment note of its variant lists them, the elements of a list of records in list order (a RecordRunProgressChange's executions in (node_id, map_index) order); an update keeps the record's position, so positions never depend on record type or database insertion order.

next_store_position: [BEHAVIOR] MUST read the counter row with load_store_position_counter for = models.StoreCounterName store_position, take one more than its last_position, or 1 when no counter row exists yet, write that number back as last_position with upsert_store_position_counter on the same repository, and return it; it is called only by this module inside the transaction of a change, so a change that fails leaves the counter as it was and no two records ever share a position.
precedent.why: State 7 defines allocation, within-change ordering, global monotonicity, and position preservation on lifecycle updates.

topics.topic: Behavior when startup cleanup of temporary or unreferenced files fails
questions: Are unreferenced file fixtures and active-run spool files left by failed calls also removed at startup, and what happens if removal of a temporary or unreferenced content file fails?
What happens when a temporary file or unreferenced value or fixture cannot be removed, since only failure to remove an obsolete spool directory is assigned behavior?

quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns StoreOpened with data_directory and temporary_files_removed, the count of temporary files removed, unnamed value files not counted; no record, named value file or spool is removed by this call; the spools of ended runs are removed later in the start sequence, by run recovery (A18 rule 4).

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
judgement.why: State 7 says unnamed fixture values are removed as unnamed value files, active-run spools are not removed by open_store, and any cleanup exception stops startup through the ordered start sequence.

topics.topic: Bootstrap behavior for missing data-store paths and objects
questions: What happens when the configured data directory, database, content-addressed areas, or spool area does not yet exist?

What happens when the data directory, database, or required subdirectories are absent, have an unexpected type, or the database is unreadable or corrupt: which are created, which refuse startup, and in what order are these checks performed?

quotes:
`refused` naming a data directory that does not exist, the lock held, a
directory not private, or a symbolic link; the start stops. The kernel never
creates the data directory itself: the owner creates it, private to the
kernel's user; inside it `open_store` creates the database schema, the
content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
judgement.why: State 7 specifies which paths must preexist, which store objects are created, the internal open-store order, and propagation of database or other startup failures.

topics.topic: Definition and enforcement of the supported Linux host boundary
questions: Must the kernel or release packaging prevent startup on a non-Linux host, or may it start there with undefined behavior because no host check is made?
Which Linux documentation or ABI version defines the required flag behavior, and who or what determines that a host satisfies it when the kernel neither names a version nor tests the behavior?

quotes:
A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another system, or
   a Linux on which an open flag these rules name (`O_NOFOLLOW`, `O_PATH`,
   `O_DIRECTORY`) does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: the
   kernel neither tests for it nor defines what it does there; the sandbox's facilities stay A03's,
   which the start probes.
judgement.why: The text explicitly names no Linux version, requires no host test, and leaves behavior undefined on non-Linux systems or Linux systems lacking the documented flag semantics.

topics.topic: Handling an existing mismatched or unreadable digest-named file
questions: When publication finds an existing file at the digest-derived destination, how does the kernel establish that its bytes and size are equal, and what happens if they differ or the existing file is unreadable?
What happens when the digest-named destination already exists but its size or bytes do not equal the bytes being published, whether because of corruption, tampering or a digest collision?

judgement.why: This is the same question about existing, missing, unreadable, corrupt or mismatched digest-named content decided in P20.

precedent.topic: Detection and handling of missing, corrupted, colliding, or otherwise damaged stored content
quotes: put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.

read_value_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise UnknownReferenceError when the identity names no record, and StoreInternalError when the bytes of an existing record are missing, unreadable, reached through a symbolic link, or differ from the record's digest or size.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
precedent.why: State 7 specifies reuse of an existing digest path, validation on reads, the resulting internal error, and startup failure propagation.

topics.topic: Lifecycle and close-on-exec requirements for traversal descriptors
questions: When are the directory and final-file descriptors closed, and must every such descriptor be close-on-exec so none can reach the sandbox or another child process?
Must every directory and final-file descriptor be close-on-exec, when must it be closed, and may any such descriptor survive into bubblewrap or another child process?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3) — the path as
   given, an absolute one walked from the root directory and a relative one
   from the working directory; each directory on the way opened with
   `O_PATH` and `O_DIRECTORY`, so a directory the kernel's user may only
   search is passed, and the last component for reading; every component the
   path names, `.` and `..` included, opened as named, and an empty one, from
   a repeated or trailing `/`, skipped; a path that names no component, empty
   or `/` alone, a file that cannot be read; a component that cannot be opened so,
   for whatever reason, making the file one that cannot be read —, and the checks and the read use
   that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.

A function never receives a credential: its environment holds only the hash
   seed (A03) and its
   inputs are values that crossed a proven edge.
judgement.divergence: One implementation closes every traversal descriptor promptly or makes it non-inheritable; another retains inheritable descriptors so a child or sandbox can access configuration or credential files, or repeated reads exhaust descriptors. The owner notices leaked protected data, failed requests or sandbox-visible host files.
judgement.why: The text fixes traversal and forbids credentials reaching functions but does not specify descriptor lifetime or inheritance controls that preserve those observable guarantees.

topics.topic: Precedence and ordering of startup refusal checks
questions: Which refusal is reported when locking, storage permissions or symlinks and another startup condition fail together?

In what order are the lock, data-directory ownership and permissions, type and symlink scan, database integrity/opening, orphan cleanup, configuration checks and sandbox probe performed, and which reason is reported when several fail?

judgement.why: This is the same question about startup validation, lock, cleanup, recovery and sandbox-check ordering decided in P21.

precedent.topic: Ordering and failure precedence of startup validation, locking, cleanup, and sandbox checks
quotes: run_start_sequence: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call, in exactly this order and each exactly once: load_installation with config_path; check_installed_instances with the loaded Installation; open_store with that Installation's data_directory; probe_sandbox; recover_in_flight_attempts; recover_running_runs (A03 rule 8, A09 rule 1, A14 rule 5, A18).

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
precedent.why: State 7 fixes both the overall startup sequence and the complete first-failure order inside store opening.

topics.topic: Resolution and symbolic-link policy for the data-directory path
questions: How is the configured data-directory path itself, including its ancestor components, opened, and may the data-directory path or an ancestor be a symbolic link?
How is the data-directory path itself and each directory component resolved, and are symbolic links in that path refused or followed before the rule against links inside the directory begins?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about resolving the data-directory path and symbolic links in its components judged in P18.

precedent.topic: Symlink and relative-path rules for traversing the data-directory path and store paths
quotes:
Every
   file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link

precedent.why: A18's store traversal requirement is unchanged; making A17's separate configuration traversal more explicit did not alter the store rule.

topics.topic: Safe flags and checks when opening the final path component
questions: Which flags are used for the final component, particularly whether `O_CLOEXEC` and `O_NONBLOCK` are required so a FIFO or other non-regular object cannot block the kernel before the regular-file check?

Which flags are used for the last component, and how is a non-regular object rejected without allowing an open of a FIFO, device or other special file to block or have side effects before the regular-file check?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3) — the path as
   given, an absolute one walked from the root directory and a relative one
   from the working directory; each directory on the way opened with
   `O_PATH` and `O_DIRECTORY`, so a directory the kernel's user may only
   search is passed, and the last component for reading; every component the
   path names, `.` and `..` included, opened as named, and an empty one, from
   a repeated or trailing `/`, skipped; a path that names no component, empty
   or `/` alone, a file that cannot be read; a component that cannot be opened so,
   for whatever reason, making the file one that cannot be read —, and the checks and the read use
   that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.
judgement.divergence: One implementation opens the final component normally and can block or trigger device behavior before learning that it is not regular; another uses nonblocking and close-on-exec protections or an equivalent safe open and promptly refuses it. The installer notices a hung or side-effecting startup, and callers notice a credential request that hangs instead of failing locally.
judgement.why: The changed traversal rule says only that the final component is opened for reading and leaves the safety flags and pre-regular-file behavior open.

precedent.topic: Cleanup or retention of fixtures and spool artifacts orphaned by failed transactions
quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns StoreOpened with data_directory and temporary_files_removed, the count of temporary files removed, unnamed value files not counted; no record, named value file or spool is removed by this call; the spools of ended runs are removed later in the start sequence, by run recovery (A18 rule 4).
precedent.why: State 7 specifies that an unreferenced fixture is an unnamed value file removed at startup, while open_store removes no spool.
